## Why the review looks like this
The half‑precision candidate uses the least energy per inference and runs fastest, so it is the cheapest option to test first on the device.
The position fine‑tune moved the success rate away from zero shift at both plus and minus three centimeters, showing a clear benefit when the start position varies.
It has not yet demonstrated stable performance at the original training mark, where the outcome remains undecided after the current trials.
Success rates compared with full precision are still too uncertain because the confidence intervals overlap the tolerance limits, so more data are needed to decide.
The deliberately miscalibrated builds fail the simple input check, which catches bad calibration before any further testing, so they are ruled out immediately.
The AI judge’s record shows it catches most failures but also raises false alarms on new objects, meaning its verdict cannot be trusted until it is re‑validated on fresh data.

## Questions to resolve before deployment
- How many additional trials per arm are required to narrow the confidence interval for the success difference between the half‑precision build and full precision to stay inside the ten‑percentage‑point tolerance?
- After more trials at the original training mark, does the position fine‑tune reach the same success level as the reference policy?
- Can the input check be adjusted to detect any remaining calibration error in the deliberately miscalibrated builds before any further testing?
- Does re‑validating the AI judge on a larger, diverse set of objects reduce its false‑alarm rate to a level that allows reliance on its verdict?
- What is the measured power consumption of the half‑precision build during continuous operation, and does it remain within the thermal envelope of the device?
